button_esd.name: button_esd
button_esd.summary: A push button to ground behind a TVS and a series resistor, for a button on the board's edge under a finger
button_esd.note: From simple_earring rev 2 (vendored with the bolt earring: boards/bolt-earring/vendor/simple_earring/scripts/circuit.py, whose comments give the reasons and the corner simulations behind each value). The TVS clamps a discharge at the switch's pad; R_SER then limits what reaches the node behind it (at a ~14 V clamp, ~14 mA through 1 kohm), which should have a capacitor of its own (power_latch's C_DEB) so a strike does not register as a press. R_SER costs a few tens of mV on the pressed level.

divider.name: divider
divider.summary: A resistive divider to an ADC input, with an optional filter capacitor
divider.note: OUT = TOP x bottom / (top + bottom). A large pair costs little current but is slow and loads easily: filter = 1 adds 100 nF from OUT to ground, which the ADC's sampling capacitor then charges from. The bolt earring has two: its battery reading (1M : 1M with the filter, on the latched cell so it reads 0 with the latch off) and its VBUS sense (10k : 10k, stiff on purpose: it holds a dead VBUS low, which the power path's gate needs). The RP2350's ADC input is a switched capacitor of about 1 pF, at least 100 kohm effective at its full 500 kS/s: a divider whose own resistance (top and bottom in parallel) is near that wants the filter, which holds OUT while each sample is taken.

filter.note: 1 for a 100 nF capacitor on OUT

citations.quote: The ADC input is capacitive. When sampling, the ADC places about 1pF across the input. Packaging, PCB routing, and other external factors introduce additional capacitance. The effective impedance, even when sampling at 500 kS/s, is over 100 kΩ. DC measurements have no need to buffer.

citations.note: Minimum ADC input impedance.

enable_or.name: enable_or
enable_or.summary: A regulator enable that is on when either of two sources is: a latched cell (through a diode) or USB (through a divider), clamped to the cell
enable_or.note: From simple_earring rev 2 (vendored with the bolt earring: boards/bolt-earring/vendor/simple_earring/scripts/circuit.py, whose comments give the reasons and the corner simulations behind each value). D_OR is two silicon diodes in series. The first passes A (the power latch's output: the cell) to EN, a diode drop lower; the second clamps EN to CLAMP (the cell) plus a diode drop, so EN never rises far above the regulator's input. R_TOP and R_BOT make B (USB VBUS) into EN at half of VBUS, so USB turns the regulator on whatever the latch says; R_BOT also holds EN low when neither is present. Silicon, not Schottky: a Schottky's reverse leakage into R_BOT, hot, put enough volts on EN to switch the board on by itself. The NCP730's EN must stay below VIN + 0.3 V: half of VBUS meets that only while the regulator's input is at least VBUS/2 - 0.3 V.

D_OR.note: Two diodes in series: 1 anode of the first, 3 their midpoint, 2 cathode of the second

CLAMP.note: The cell: EN is clamped a diode drop above it

led.note: The resistor is the smallest stocked value that holds the LED to current_a at its lowest forward voltage (and so below its own maximum current). led_chain.name: led_chain
led_chain.summary: A chain of addressable LEDs (WS2816C-1313), data from one to the next, with bypass capacitors
led_chain.note: Each LED's DO feeds the next one's DI. The datasheet contradicts itself on capacitors (none needed, p.1; 100 nF suggested between VDD and GND, p.5): cap_every = 1 puts one by every LED, larger values one by every that-many, starting at LED cap_first (the bolt earring starts at the 4th and puts one by every 6th, so each sits mid-group). DI's thresholds are fractions of VDD, so a 3.3 V output can't drive a chain at a LiPo's 4.2 V directly (0.7 x 4.2 = 2.94 V): the level rule says so, and nfet_level_shift is the usual fix. The footprint is simple_earring's (library parts.pretty, vendored with the bolt earring); KiCad's LED:WS2812B symbol has the same pin numbers.

light_sensor.name: light_sensor
light_sensor.summary: An ambient-light phototransistor (ALS-PT19) with its load resistor and filter capacitor, to an ADC input
light_sensor.note: The phototransistor's collector is on VDD and its emitter drives OUT, loaded by R_LOAD and filtered by C_FILT. The output is the photocurrent times R_LOAD, until it saturates near VDD: a larger load reads dimmer light and saturates sooner. The bolt earring uses 22 kohm, from simple_earring rev 2 (vendored with the bolt earring: boards/bolt-earring/vendor/simple_earring/scripts/circuit.py): about 0.33 V at 100 lux, saturating near 900 lux. Mount it facing out, away from LEDs it would read.

lipo_load_share.name: lipo_load_share
lipo_load_share.summary: Load sharing for a 1S LiPo and its charger: the system runs from the input when it is present and from the cell when not
lipo_load_share.note: Microchip AN1149's circuit. With input power present, Q1's gate is at VIN and it is off, so the system draws from VIN through D1 and the charger sees only the cell; a load on the cell would keep the charge current from ever falling to the termination value. Without input, R_GATE pulls the gate to ground and Q1 connects the cell to the system (its body diode already conducts). D1 keeps the cell from back-feeding VIN. Q1: drain at the cell, source at VSYS. Two departures the bolt earring makes (simple_earring rev 2, whose reasons are in its circuit script, vendored at boards/bolt-earring/vendor/simple_earring/scripts/circuit.py): a silicon D1 (diode = 1n4007ws), because a Schottky's reverse leakage from VSYS into a dead VBUS, hot, lifted VBUS far enough to switch the board on by itself, at the price of about 0.8 V drop instead of 0.3 V; and the gate fed through R_SERIES from VIN (series_ohm), so the gate is a divider R_SERIES : R_GATE that sits at nearly VIN with input present. Without input the gate follows the dead VIN node down, so VIN must be held low by something (the bolt's VBUS-sense divider does it): a floating VIN near the cell's voltage would leave Q1 off and the board running only from USB.

Q1.note: P-channel: gate VIN (or the divider), source VSYS, drain the cell

R_GATE.note: RPULL: pulls Q1's gate low when the input is absent

D1.note: VIN to VSYS while input power is present

BAT.note: The cell's positive terminal, where the charger's output is

VSYS.note: The system load: VIN less D1's drop, or the cell

citations.note: The circuit: P-MOSFET Q1 with its gate at VIN and RPULL to ground, Schottky D1 from VIN to the load.

citations.quote: If the system draws current from the battery, the charge current will never meet the termination value. This causes the non-termination of the charge management circuit.

long_press_reset.name: long_press_reset
long_press_reset.summary: Hold a button for seconds to reset an RP2350 into its USB bootloader: an RC timer, a Schmitt buffer, and two N-FETs on BOOTSEL and RUN
long_press_reset.note: From simple_earring rev 2 (vendored with the bolt earring: boards/bolt-earring/vendor/simple_earring/scripts/circuit.py, whose comments give the reasons and the corner simulations behind each value), where it replaced the BOOTSEL key. IN is high while the button is held (power_latch's PRESSED). R_TMR charges C_TMR (tau 6.8 s nominal; simple_earring's corners give 2-11 s) and D_DIS empties it the moment IN falls, so holds do not add up. U1, two Schmitt inverters, turns BOOT_TMR into one clean rising edge on LONG. LONG drives Q_BOOT, which pulls BOOTSEL low (through the MCU's own 1 kohm to QSPI_SS) for as long as the button is held; C_KICK and R_KICK differentiate LONG's edge into a ~10 ms pulse on Q_RUN's gate, which pulls RUN low. The chip resets and its boot ROM finds QSPI_SS strapped low. On a battery board whose MCU holds the power latch, the reset also drops the hold, so the board turns off on release: a hardware force-off. Everything runs from VDD, so the block draws nothing with the board off. R_TMR is large so U1's input leakage stays small next to the charge current; IN's source must hold IN low against it (power_latch's R_SENSE).

D_DIS.note: 1 cathode on IN, 2 anode on BOOT_TMR

C_TMR.note: The timer's capacitor; X5R, so its value moves with temperature and bias

U1.note: 1A pin 1, 1Y pin 6, 2A pin 3, 2Y pin 4, VCC 5, GND 2

Q_BOOT.note: Pulls BOOTSEL low while LONG is high

Q_RUN.note: Pulls RUN low for the pulse

IN.note: High while the button is held

BOOTSEL.note: Open drain: to the RP2350's BOOTSEL resistor, the far end from QSPI_SS

RUN.note: Open drain: to the RP2350's RUN, which needs its pull-up

nfet_level_shift.name: nfet_level_shift
nfet_level_shift.summary: One N-MOSFET and a pull-up: a logic output shifted up to another rail, inverted
nfet_level_shift.note: The input drives the gate; the drain is pulled up to VOUT. It inverts (input high pulls the output low), so firmware sends the complement: the RP2350 can invert a pin's output in hardware (GPIO OUTOVER). The bolt earring drives its LED chains like this, with 1 kohm pull-ups. The output's high is VOUT through the pull-up: its rise time is the pull-up times the line's capacitance, so keep the pull-up small for fast data (800 kHz LED data wants well under 1 us).

Q1.note: 1 gate, 2 source, 3 drain, as KiCad's BSS138 symbol

power_latch.name: power_latch
power_latch.summary: A push-on soft power latch for a battery board: a button press switches the cell through, the MCU holds it on, and the press is readable as a clean logic level
power_latch.note: From simple_earring rev 2 (vendored with the bolt earring: boards/bolt-earring/vendor/simple_earring/scripts/circuit.py, whose comments give the reasons and the corner simulations behind each value). Q_SW, a P-FET, switches the cell to OUT when its gate (LATCH_G) is pulled low; R_GATE holds it off. Pressing the button pulls BTN low, which pulls LATCH_G low through one anode of D_OR, so the board comes on; the MCU then drives HOLD high and Q_HOLD keeps LATCH_G low after the button is released. R_HOLD keeps HOLD low until firmware drives it, so the latch is off at boot and while the MCU is in reset. D_OR's other anode pulls PRESS_N low on a press; Q_SENSE, a P-FET from VIO, turns that into PRESSED, high while the button is held (a P-FET because the diode's low, about 0.45 V, is too near a Schmitt input's threshold but is plenty of gate drive). R_SENSE pulls PRESSED low: the MCU pin's own pull-up must be off. C_DEB debounces the button (R_GATE x C_DEB, 10 ms, on release) and is the second ESD stage behind button_esd. Q_SW carries only what OUT feeds (an enable line and a divider in the bolt), so a weak part with a high threshold is chosen: leakage into LATCH_G with the board off must not reach its threshold, hot.

Q_HOLD.note: The MCU's hold: drain on LATCH_G

R_HOLD.note: HOLD low until firmware drives it: off at boot

D_OR.note: Two diodes, common cathode (3) on BTN: anode 2 on LATCH_G, anode 1 on PRESS_N

C_DEB.note: Debounce, and the second ESD stage

Q_SENSE.note: P-channel inverter: source VIO, drain PRESSED

OUT.note: The cell while the latch is on: an enable line and light loads, not the system current

BTN.note: The button's node: pulled low (through button_esd) to press

PRESSED.note: High while the button is held

usb_c_sink.name: usb_c_sink
usb_c_sink.summary: USB-C receptacle as a USB 2.0 sink: 5 V from the host, D+/D-, and Rd on each CC pin
usb_c_sink.note: A device that only takes power and USB 2.0 data. Each CC pin has its own 5.1 kohm pull-down (Rd) so the source turns VBUS on whichever way the plug is turned; the two must not share one resistor. 1 % parts meet both the 20 % tolerance that only asks for default power and the 10 % one a sink needs to read the source's advertised current. Both D+ pads and both D- pads are joined at the receptacle, so either plug orientation works. The receptacle's pin names are KiCad 9's (its shield pin is S1; KiCad 10 calls it SH). No ESD protection: add it on boards a person plugs by hand often.

VBUS.note: The host's 5 V. Default USB power's range is the USB 2.0 specification's (not read); 4.75-5.5 V unloaded is what a Type-C Current source must give, and up to 5.5 V is what a legacy device may see at light load

usb.note: The cable's far end is a host, so a device's USB connects here.

citations.quote: Both CC1 and CC2 pins shall be independently terminated to ground through Rd.

citations.note: The column is whether the sink can detect the source's power capability; the ±10 % 5.1 kΩ row says Yes.

citations.quote: The allowable default range for VBUS as measured at the Source receptacle shall be as defined by the USB 2.0 and USB 3.2 specifications.
shall output a voltage in the range of 4.75 V – 5.5 V when no current is being drawn

stock.note: Parts a recipe can choose by value (a recipe part's `choose`). Each table is one footprint and one maker's series; `si` is the value in SI units. LCSC numbers, JLC library type and stock were read with jlc_parts.py (easy_pcb's pcb-design skill) on the date in `checked`; only basic and preferred parts (no extended-part fee) are listed.

resistor_0402.note: UNI-ROYAL 0402WGF series, 1 %, 1/16 W, 0402. E12 and the common E24 values JLC stocks as basic or preferred; 27 and 68 ohm are extended and left out.

interfaces.note: Interface types: the bundles of signals a package's interfaces are instances of (each package's ports.json, under "interfaces"). Signals are named from the device's own side, so two devices connect by the type's joins: one's SDO to the other's SDI. Where a signal has a direction, it is the controller's; a target's is the reverse. Whether a connection needs more than wires (pull-ups, a level shifter) is for interface rules, not these types.

i2c.note: A bus: any number of targets on one controller's two lines, each at its own address.

pullup.note: One pull-up per line to the bus's rail, between Rp(min) = (V - VOL) / IOL and Rp(max) = tr / (0.8473 * Cb), for the mode of the bus's slowest device (its max_khz). Table 2-1 gives VOL at a 3 mA sink for all three modes. Cb is estimated as pin_pf per device plus wiring_pf; both are assumptions, not cited figures, and a connection's bus_pf replaces the estimate.

spi.note: A bus: targets share SCK, SDO and SDI, and each has its own CS. A device that only listens or only talks needs one data line.

uart.note: Point to point. Flow control (RTS, CTS) is optional, as is either direction.

pwm.note: One PWM slice: two channels at one frequency. Either channel alone will do.

logic.note: One digital line. An instance says which way it goes (dir: in, out, bidir) and how it drives (push_pull, open_drain, tristate).

pio.note: A programmable I/O block: on any pins it reaches, software state machines can act as any digital interface (it lists them under implements). Use one only when no hardware block fits: it costs state machines and firmware.
